segments.t: KorTTY provides a tabbed terminal interface with support for multiple simultaneous SSH connections, split-screen layouts, and interactive terminal management features. This guide covers tab operations, multi-window support, terminal customization, and advanced session features.
The following diagram shows the terminal tab and session lifecycle, including split-screen and broadcast modes.
Manage multiple SSH sessions with these tab operations:
KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003+KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 (Cmd+T on macOS) — opens Quick Connect to start a new session

KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003+KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 (Cmd+W on macOS) — closes the active tab. You are only asked to confirm when there is something to lose: the tab has split panes, or a command is still running (a local shell with a running child process, or an SSH session that is not at its prompt). An idle single terminal closes immediately. The per-connection KTPH006Close without confirmationKTPH007 setting suppresses the prompt entirely.

Right-click a tab, the terminal area, or a server entry in the Dashboard. If the connection is active, it is closed and re-established immediately; if disconnected, it is re-established. The terminal window stays open.
Right-click a tab to assign it to a named group for better organization

Interactive SSH terminals share host-key trust with SFTP and the SSH bootstrap used by Mosh. The first connection to a normalized host and port shows the key algorithm and OpenSSH SHA-256 fingerprint with KTPH000NoKTPH001 selected by default. After you verify and accept it, exact matches connect silently; a changed key is hard-blocked with no automatic retry. See KTPH002SSH host-key verificationKTPH003.

Opening a same-server or newly selected connection in a split shows a progress dialog while the SSH handshake runs on a worker. The interface remains responsive for both the host-key confirmation and keyboard-interactive authentication prompts.

Some failures are refused outright rather than retried, because repeating the attempt cannot change the outcome — a changed host key, a Mosh connection configured with a jump server, or a missing Mosh runtime. The terminal clears and shows the reason immediately instead of working through the retry count. See KTPH000Jump serverKTPH001 for the Mosh restriction.

KorTTY's pinned SithTermFX build also includes a reviewed bottom-row boundary fix: moving over a hyperlink or the final visible terminal row no longer asks KTPH000 for the non-existent row at KTPH001.

When an KTPH004establishedKTPH005 SSH connection is lost — network drop, VPN cut, server gone — the tab does KTPH006notKTPH007 close. It switches to a red disconnected state instead: the tab title gets a KTPH000 suffix, the tab turns dark red, a red status bar shows the time the connection was lost, and the terminal cursor stops blinking so a dead session no longer looks alive. Only a normal remote logout (typing KTPH001, or KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011 at the prompt) closes the tab.

KorTTY notices a silent transport death within about ten seconds: every few seconds it sends an SSH liveness probe (a global request the server must answer, the same technique as OpenSSH's KTPH000) and treats two consecutive unanswered probes as a lost connection. The probe only arms itself after the server has answered once, so servers that never reply to such requests keep their sessions untouched. This is independent of the KTPH001SSH keep-aliveKTPH002 heartbeat, which keeps idle connections open but does not detect a dead one.

To pick the session back up in the same tab, double-click the red status bar or the red tab, or use KTPH000ReconnectKTPH001 in the tab, terminal, or Dashboard context menu. In a split tab, panes whose connection died close individually; the last remaining pane keeps the tab open and carries the reconnect offer.

With KTPH000Automatically reconnect lost connectionsKTPH001 enabled (KTPH002Settings → TerminalKTPH003, on by default), the tab reconnects on its own: attempts start after 3 seconds and back off through 5, 10, 20 and 30 seconds up to one attempt per minute, and the red status bar counts down to the next attempt. A successful reconnect, a manual reconnect, or closing the tab ends the automatic attempts. Permanent failures — authentication, host-key verification, configuration refusals — stop them too, so a wrong password is never hammered against the server. While a KTPH004session journalKTPH005 is running, its red decision bar takes precedence and no automatic attempt starts — the journal asks whether to reconnect and continue or to end with its closing summary. See KTPH006Settings → TerminalKTPH007 for the setting.
Open additional windows to organize connections by project or environment:
KTPH003New WindowKTPH004: KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 (Cmd+Shift+N on macOS) opens a new KorTTY window. Each window can have its own set of tabs and connections.

KTPH000Move tabs between windowsKTPH001: Drag a tab from the tab bar and drop it onto another KorTTY window's tab bar to move that tab (and its session, including any split terminals) into the other window.
KTPH000Reorder tabsKTPH001: Drag a tab within the same window to change its order; the "+" tab stays at the end.
Adjust the font size of the active terminal on the fly without reconnecting:
Zoom in/out over the terminal (Cmd + wheel on macOS)

Holding KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009 (or KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011 on macOS) and scrolling the mouse wheel over the terminal changes the font size — wheel up enlarges, wheel down shrinks — instead of scrolling the buffer. This complements the KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 / KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 / KTPH020KTPH006KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH007KTPH023 shortcuts.

KTPH000Reset zoomKTPH001 restores the font size and family to what the connection had when you opened the tab (or the connection's saved settings, or the global default). The same reset is available via the terminal context menu: right-click → KTPH002Font sizeKTPH003 → KTPH004ResetKTPH005. The zoom level applies only to the currently focused terminal.

KTPH000View → Zoom → Background TransparencyKTPH001 is a slider (0–100 %) that makes the terminal background see-through to the desktop while the text stays fully opaque and sharp. At 0 % the background is solid; higher values let more of the desktop show through. The value is saved and restored across restarts.
Only the terminal area becomes transparent — the title bar, menu bar, status bar and any tab without a terminal stay solid, so the window never turns into a see-through hole.

Horizontal, vertical and nested split terminals inherit the active transparency level, including panes added after transparency was enabled. Entering fullscreen with KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 or terminal-only fullscreen with KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011 temporarily renders the terminal area opaque without changing the saved value; leaving fullscreen restores that value to every pane.

Because a see-through window uses a different window style that the operating system fixes when the window opens, KTPH000switching transparency on or off (crossing 0 %) only takes full effect after a restartKTPH001; the status bar shows a hint when you cross that threshold. Adjusting the level while already in transparent mode applies live. In transparent mode the window uses a lightweight custom title bar (drag to move, buttons to minimise/maximise/close, double-click the strip to maximise, drag the edges to resize).
The slider lives in the in-window menu bar only (the native macOS menu bar cannot host a slider).

Besides SSH and Mosh, a terminal tab can host a KTPH000Local ShellKTPH001 — the local machine's own shell, opened via a pseudo-terminal (see KTPH002Local ShellKTPH003). A few terminal behaviors are local-shell aware:

KTPH006KTPH007KTPH000KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH001KTPH010 closes the tab for local cmd.exe/PowerShell sessions.KTPH011 Those Windows shells do not exit on EOF, so KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 would otherwise have no effect. For bash-family shells (Git Bash/Cygwin/WSL, macOS/Linux) and SSH, KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 keeps its normal EOF meaning — the shell exits and the local tab then auto-closes.

KTPH000Close confirmationKTPH001 uses local-shell wording rather than "End SSH connection?", and the window-close prompt is transport-neutral ("Active sessions"), since one window can mix SSH, Mosh and local-shell tabs.

KTPH004The current directory follows the interactive shell.KTPH005 On macOS and Linux, korTTY refreshes it from the local shell process; native PowerShell and cmd prompts supply absolute Windows paths. After KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, or KTPH003, KTPH006Open in Snippet EditorKTPH007 resolves a selected file name against that current directory instead of the tab's start directory. If the directory cannot be determined or mapped safely, korTTY stops with an error rather than opening a same-named file from the wrong directory.

KTPH006After an identity switch, Open in Snippet Editor is greyed out.KTPH007 When the session no longer runs as the identity the tab was opened with — after KTPH000, an inner KTPH001, or a shell-opening KTPH002 — the context-menu entry is disabled, in SSH tabs as well as local-shell tabs: the tab's tracked directories and file access still belong to the original login and would resolve the wrong path. The entry re-enables on its own once the prompt shows the original user again (typically after KTPH003). A local-shell tab whose configured shell command is itself a remote client such as KTPH004 or KTPH005 keeps the entry disabled for the whole tab. If the load is triggered anyway, korTTY stops with an error instead of resolving the wrong path.

KTPH001Clipboard text is preserved in agent shortcuts.KTPH002 Typed and pasted text travel through the same terminal-input filter, including bracketed paste and split UTF-8 input, so a pasted file name remains part of the KTPH000 request and Enter dispatches it exactly once.

Every terminal tab can keep a KTPH000session journalKTPH001: server output and typed commands go into a capture log, an AI condenses them into a readable timeline, and screenshots and notes can be added from the journal bar or the terminal's right-click menu. Journals start automatically for connections that enable them, or retroactively for a running session via KTPH002Tools KTPH006 Start/Stop Session JournalKTPH003 — the existing scrollback is imported. See KTPH004Session journalKTPH005.
Split the terminal view to display multiple connections side by side, and optionally send input to all panes at once.
KTPH000Split PaneKTPH001: Create horizontal or vertical splits within a tab via the context menu or keyboard shortcuts.
KTPH000Independent SessionsKTPH001: Each pane can show a different SSH connection.
KTPH000Resizable PanesKTPH001: Drag dividers to adjust pane sizes.

KTPH000Access reason asked once per tabKTPH001: when a server asks for a reason for the connection, as a CyberArk-style jump host does, a split does not ask again. korTTY sends the reason that was given when the tab was opened, because a server that asks for one closes a session that answers with nothing. A split to a different server, or a server asking something else, is asked once as well, and a new tab always starts by asking. If the server refuses the reason, for example because a ticket number has expired in the meantime, korTTY drops it and asks again on the next attempt.

KTPH004Move PanesKTPH005: Hold KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 (Windows/Linux) or KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013 (macOS) and drag a pane onto another to reorder. Without the modifiers, mouse drag is used for text selection in the terminal.
When KTPH000Broadcast ModeKTPH001 is enabled, keyboard input is sent simultaneously to all visible panes. This is useful for running the same commands on multiple servers.
Terminal effects can change the visible terminal style and output animation. Effects are Java plugins managed from KTPH000Plugins KTPH002 Terminal EffectsKTPH001.
KTPH000Current terminalKTPH001: Use KTPH002View KTPH004 Terminal EffectKTPH003 or the terminal context menu to choose an effect for the active terminal.
KTPH000Quick ConnectKTPH001: Choose the effect and speed before opening a temporary or saved connection.
KTPH000Connection ManagerKTPH001: Store the effect and speed on a saved connection so new tabs use it automatically.
KTPH003SpeedKTPH004: Use the slider for KTPH000 through KTPH001; if that is still too slow, type a custom value up to KTPH002 in the numeric speed field.
Open KTPH000Plugins KTPH002 Terminal EffectsKTPH001 to manage plugins.
The table lists loaded plugins with active state, name, and description.
KTPH000DisableKTPH001 a plugin to keep it installed but unavailable for activation.
KTPH002ImportKTPH003 external KTPH000 plugins. KorTTY copies them into KTPH001.
KTPH000ExportKTPH001 plugins that have a source JAR. The bundled MOTHER effect is exportable.
Imported terminal-effect plugins are trusted Java code and are not sandboxed. Only import plugins from sources you trust.
For detailed plugin development documentation, see KTPH000Terminal effect pluginsKTPH001.
Prevent connections from dropping due to inactivity by configuring SSH keep-alive messages:
Enable KTPH000SSH Keep-AliveKTPH001 in the connection's KTPH002TerminalKTPH003 tab or in KTPH004Settings KTPH006 TerminalKTPH005.
Set the interval (5 to 600 seconds, default: 60).
KorTTY sends KTPH000 heartbeat messages at the configured interval and enables TCP socket keepalive while the option is active.

If a server, firewall, VPN, or NAT gateway closes idle sessions sooner than the configured interval, the connection can still end. In that case, check the server-side SSH configuration and network idle-timeout settings as well as the KorTTY log.

Writes a connection's terminal output to a file, for audit and debugging. This is independent of the KTPH000Session JournalKTPH001: it is a plain transcript with no summaries, markers or screenshots, and the two can run at the same time.
KTPH000Connection Manager KTPH002 Edit connection KTPH003 LoggingKTPH001 for a saved connection.
KTPH000Quick Connect KTPH002 Terminal logKTPH001 for a one-off session, or to change the setting for the connection you are about to open.
Choose a KTPH001log folderKTPH002. Left empty, KorTTY uses KTPH000. You pick the folder; the file names are KorTTY's.
KTPH000Plain TextKTPH001 - One timestamped line per line of output.

Optionally adjust the KTPH000maximum file sizeKTPH001 (default: 10 MB) and the KTPH002retention periodKTPH003 (default: 30 days), and turn off KTPH004Start a new file every dayKTPH005 or KTPH006Compress closed files (gzip)KTPH007 — both are on by default. Quick Connect's Terminal log section covers enable, folder, format and compression; size limit, retention and daily rotation keep their configured or default values.

Every file is named KTPH000, for example KTPH001. The date leads so a folder listing sorts chronologically, and the trailing number distinguishes connections that are open at the same time — two tabs on the same server get KTPH002 and KTPH003 and never write into one another's file.

By default a new file is started KTPH002every dayKTPH003, and always again whenever the maximum size is reached (those parts are numbered KTPH000, KTPH001, …); daily rotation can be turned off to roll only by size. Nothing is ever overwritten or deleted by rotation.

Closed files are gzipped by default; the file currently being written always stays uncompressed so that a crash cannot truncate it. Turn off KTPH000Compress closed files (gzip)KTPH001 to keep finished files as plain text instead. A connection that produces no output creates no file at all.

Files older than the retention period are deleted automatically when a connection starts and after each daily rollover. Set the retention to KTPH000 to keep everything. Only KorTTY's own log files are ever removed — anything else in the folder is left alone, so it is safe to point the setting at a folder you also use for other things.

Captured lines go through the same redaction as the KTPH000Session JournalKTPH001, on the capture thread, before anything is buffered or written: the connection's own password and any replacement rules your organisation's policy defines. The secret never reaches the file, so there is nothing to clean up afterwards.
Log files and a log folder KorTTY created itself are set to owner-only permissions where the filesystem supports it. A folder you chose yourself is left with the permissions you gave it.
Redaction only covers what KorTTY knows

A password KorTTY stores for the connection is redacted. A secret you type into a command yourself, or one a program prints, is not — KorTTY has no way to recognise it. Treat the log folder as sensitive, and use policy replacement rules for patterns that recur.

Terminal recording is designed as a low-resource replay feature. KorTTY records terminal screen-state changes and timing events into one JDK/GZIP streaming-compressed KTPH000 file per terminal tab session. Legacy KTPH001 replay files remain readable.
To enable recording automatically after every app restart, open KTPH000Settings KTPH004 VideoKTPH001 and enable KTPH002Enable terminal recording after app restartKTPH003.
To enable recording only for this session, open KTPH000Tools KTPH004 Video Manager...KTPH001 and select KTPH002Enable terminal recording for this app sessionKTPH003.
Set the KTPH001Storage pathKTPH002. If left at the default, KorTTY uses KTPH000.
Choose the default format and default split scope. KorTTY replay is always available; video export requires KTPH000.
Enable or disable KTPH000Auto-pause when the terminal is idleKTPH001 and set the idle threshold (default: 20 seconds).
Optional: enable KTPH000Capture terminal colors in new recordingsKTPH001 if exported videos should reproduce terminal colors.
Optional: set the KTPH000 path and click KTPH002CheckKTPH003. If KTPH001 is missing, video export stays disabled but replay files remain usable.
Open or focus an SSH terminal tab.

If terminal recording is enabled, click KTPH003Start recordingKTPH004 in the terminal bar, choose KTPH005Tools KTPH013 Start/Stop Terminal RecordingKTPH006, or press KTPH007KTPH000KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH001KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH002KTPH012 (Cmd+Shift+E on macOS).
If the tab contains multiple split terminals, choose whether to record only the active split or the whole tab.
Click KTPH003Stop recordingKTPH004 or press KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 again to stop the current segment.
Start and stop as often as needed in the same tab. KorTTY appends all segments to the same replay file until the tab closes.
Select a KTPH000 replay file from the list.
Verify that the ffmpeg status says video export is enabled.
Choose KTPH001Export entire recordingKTPH002 or enter start/end times with minute or KTPH000 format.
Choose whether to include terminal colors (available only if the replay contains color data).
Choose KTPH000WebM/VP9KTPH001 or KTPH002MKV/FFV1KTPH003 format, then select an output path.

While KorTTY renders frames and runs KTPH000, the export progress dialog shows the current phase, progress bar, and estimated remaining time. Export uses the recorded terminal geometry so large terminal screens are not cropped.
Click KTPH000ViewKTPH001 to play the replay directly inside KorTTY.
Use the replay viewer timeline to scrub, or enter a KTPH002Time jumpKTPH003 value such as KTPH000 for minute 5 or KTPH001 for minute 5 and 30 seconds.
Set KTPH002SpeedKTPH003 between KTPH000 and KTPH001 to control playback speed.
Click KTPH000Rename...KTPH001 to rename the replay file.
Click KTPH000DeleteKTPH001 to delete the selected replay after confirmation.
